title: Forces & Newton's laws
examples: How do I find the tension in a rope connecting two masses?
Can you show me how to resolve a force into horizontal and vertical parts?
What is the difference between net force and the force applied?

explain.say: Today we look at forces and Newton's laws. First we learn to resolve forces into components. This means breaking one force into two parts. These parts are usually horizontal and vertical. For example if a force of ten newtons acts at an angle, we find its x and y parts. We use trigonometry for this calculation.

Next we use Newton's second law. This law states that the net force equals mass times acceleration. We write this as F equals ma. Remember to use the net force, which is the total force acting on the object. If the net force is zero, the acceleration must also be zero.

Finally we look at connected particles. This means two or more objects are linked together by ropes or strings. We must treat the system as a whole or analyze each particle separately. For example if two masses are connected by a string, the tension in the string is the force we need to find. We apply F equals ma to each mass individually.

faq.q: What is the net force if two forces pull at right angles?
faq.a: You find the net force using the Pythagorean theorem. You square the two perpendicular forces, add them, and then take the square root. Another way to ask this is what is the resultant force? Or how do I find the magnitude of perpendicular forces?
asks: How do I find the magnitude of perpendicular forces?

faq.q: When do I use F equals ma?
faq.a: You use this equation whenever there is an acceleration or a net force acting on an object. If the object is stationary or moving at a constant speed, the net force is zero. You could also ask when is the net force zero? Or how do I calculate acceleration from forces?
asks: When is the net force zero?
How do I calculate acceleration from forces?

faq.q: How do I find the tension in a system?
faq.a: You must apply Newton's second law to the specific particle where you want to find the tension. The tension force will be one of the forces you include in the net force calculation. You might also ask how do I find the tension in a rope? Or what is the tension force?
asks: How do I find the tension in a rope?

faq.q: Do I need to draw a diagram for force resolution?
faq.a: Yes, drawing a clear free-body diagram is very important. It helps you correctly identify all the forces acting on the object. You can also ask what should I draw for forces? Or how do I set up the diagram?
asks: What should I draw for forces?
How do I set up the diagram?

faq.q: Is the tension the same throughout a connected rope?
faq.a: No, the tension can change if the masses are accelerating differently. You must calculate the tension separately for each section or particle. You could also ask does tension change along the rope? Or is tension constant?
asks: Does tension change along the rope?

facts: Newton's second law states that net force equals mass times acceleration.
Resolving a force means breaking it into perpendicular components, like x and y.
If the net force on an object is zero, the object is either stationary or moving at a constant velocity.
Tension is the force transmitted through a string or cable connecting two objects.

quiz.say: A force of fifteen newtons acts at an angle of sixty degrees above the horizontal. What is its horizontal component?
quiz.why: The horizontal component is found using the cosine function, so fifteen times the cosine of sixty degrees equals seven point five newtons.

wrong.1: This uses the sine function, which calculates the vertical component, not the horizontal one.
wrong.2: This incorrectly uses the sine angle value instead of the given sixty degrees.
wrong.3: This assumes the force is acting purely horizontally, ignoring the angle given.

quiz.say: A block is pulled across a surface by a force of twenty newtons at an angle of thirty degrees. If the block has a mass of ten kilograms, what is the acceleration?
quiz.why: You must find the net force first by resolving the applied force, and then divide that net force by the mass to find acceleration.

wrong.0: This only calculates the horizontal component of the force and ignores the angle.
wrong.1: This calculates the net force but forgets to divide by the mass to find acceleration.
wrong.2: This assumes the force is acting purely horizontally and ignores the mass entirely.
